title: Gossip & Failure Detection
subtitle: Watch a cluster notice a dead node, spread the news by rumor, and then get fooled by a network split.
learn: How heartbeats let one node judge whether another is alive
Why a fixed timeout is a blunt tool and what a phi-accrual detector does instead
How gossip spreads membership news to every node in roughly log N rounds
Why, over an unreliable network, a failure detector can only suspect and never know, and how that causes false alarms
What split brain is and why a majority rule contains it

steps.title: Is that node dead or just quiet?
steps.body: A five-node cluster stores data and must route around machines that fail. One node, A, is the leader that coordinates writes. But no node can look at another's power light. All it can see is messages arriving or not arriving. Silence could mean a crash, a slow disk, a long garbage-collection pause (the program freezes while it cleans up memory), or a broken network cable. This lesson shows how a cluster turns silence into a decision.
steps.idea: Over an unreliable network, failure detection is a guess from missing messages, never a direct observation.
steps.caption: Five peers and a client. Nobody can see another node's health.

steps.title: Heartbeats
steps.body: Each node sends a tiny heartbeat message ("I'm alive") to its peers on a schedule, say once per second. Every receiver records when the last one arrived. As long as beats keep landing about a second apart, the sender is presumed healthy. Here E sends beats #41 and #42 to D. A heartbeat only proves the sender could send a moment ago, not that it is doing useful work. Big clusters limit the cost: each node beats to only a few peers, or the counter rides on gossip messages.
steps.idea: A heartbeat is a regular "I am alive" message. Its absence is the only warning sign.
steps.caption: E sends a heartbeat to D every second, and D logs each arrival.

steps.title: The fixed timeout
steps.body: Now E crashes and its heartbeats stop. The simplest rule is a fixed timeout: if no heartbeat arrives for 5 seconds, declare E dead. It is easy to understand but rigid. On a quiet local network, 5 seconds is slower than it needs to be. On a congested or cross-region link where delays vary a lot, 5 seconds will wrongly fire on healthy nodes. One number cannot suit every network or every moment.
steps.idea: A fixed timeout trades detection speed against false alarms, and the right value changes with conditions.
steps.caption: E has crashed. D waits for the 5 s timer to expire.

steps.title: Phi-accrual detection
steps.body: A phi-accrual detector (used by Cassandra and Akka) learns how late beats normally are. It reports a suspicion score, phi, that grows as silence continues. Phi 1 means a gap this long would happen about 10% of the time if the node were healthy. Phi 2 is about 1%, and phi 8 about one in a hundred million. With a 1 s average gap, threshold 8 needs about 18.4 s of silence. That is slower than the 5 s rule on a steady link, because 8 is deliberately cautious. The gain is that the same threshold stretches on a jittery link (4 s average gives about 74 s) and tightens on a fast one (100 ms average gives about 1.8 s). A lower threshold detects sooner but causes more false alarms.
steps.idea: Phi adapts to the network's observed jitter and gives a graded suspicion level, not a plain yes or no.
steps.caption: Silence grows, and phi climbs past the threshold of 8.

steps.title: Gossip starts
steps.body: D now suspects E, but every node must end up with the same view of who is alive. Instead of D messaging everyone, nodes gossip: every second, each node picks a few random peers and swaps what it knows, tagging each fact with a version number. D tells B and C that E looks down. Cassandra gossips heartbeat counters and each node judges for itself. SWIM-style systems (SWIM is a gossip membership protocol) gossip the suspicion itself, as here. New nodes join through a seed node, and no coordinator is needed.
steps.idea: Gossip means each node regularly swaps its knowledge with random peers, with no central coordinator.
steps.caption: D tells two random peers that E is suspected.

steps.title: The rumor spreads
steps.body: In the next round, B and C each pick their own random peers, and A hears the news. With one peer per round, the number of informed nodes roughly doubles in the early rounds. So news reaches N nodes in about log2(N) rounds, plus a few more for stragglers: roughly 15 to 17 rounds for 1,000 nodes. Contacting a few peers per round makes it faster. Each node sends the same small number of messages per round however big the cluster is.
steps.idea: Informed nodes roughly double each early round, so spread time grows with log N while each node's load stays flat.
steps.caption: A, B, C and D now all know. The live cluster agrees.

steps.title: False alarms
steps.body: Suppose in an alternate run that E is fine, but a 20 s garbage-collection pause froze it. Its heartbeats stop, phi passes 8, and the cluster marks it down, though E is healthy. When E wakes up it can refute the rumor. In SWIM, a suspect raises its incarnation number (a counter only that node increments), and the higher number overwrites the suspicion in gossip. SWIM also uses indirect probes: other nodes ping the suspect for you, which avoids false alarms from one bad link. A too-sensitive threshold causes flapping, where nodes are shunned and readmitted and data moves for nothing. A too-lax one leaves real failures undetected longer.
steps.idea: A detector is never certain. The threshold balances slow detection against false alarms.
steps.caption: In this alternate run E was only paused, yet all four peers think it is down until it refutes.

steps.title: Split brain
steps.body: Now a network partition cuts the cluster in two. A, B and C can talk to each other, and so can D and E, but the two groups cannot reach each other. Each side sees the other go silent and decides it is the survivor. If both sides elect their own leader and accept writes, you get split brain: two active leaders with diverging data. Here a client writes x=1 to A and another write x=2 lands on E, so the two sides now disagree.
steps.idea: Split brain is when both halves of a partition believe they alone are in charge.
steps.caption: Both sides suspect the other and each has a leader. Clients write to both.

steps.title: Containing it with a majority
steps.body: The usual defence is a quorum rule: only a group holding a strict majority of the configured members (3 of 5 here) may act as leader or accept writes. The 2-node side can still tell it lost contact, so it steps down or goes read-only. Two separate groups can never both hold a majority, so at most one side can elect a leader or commit writes. A stale leader on the minority side may linger briefly, so real systems add terms, leases and fencing, covered in later lessons.
steps.idea: Detection only suspects. A majority rule lets at most one side make progress, because two majorities always overlap.
steps.caption: A, B and C keep the majority. D and E refuse writes.

steps.title: From silence to decision
steps.body: Heartbeats make silence measurable. Phi-accrual turns the length of that silence into a graded suspicion that adapts to the network. Gossip spreads the verdict to every node in about log N rounds with no coordinator. Because any verdict can be wrong, safety-critical actions such as electing a leader need a majority, not just one detector's opinion.
steps.idea: Detect with heartbeats, spread with gossip, and act only with a majority.
steps.caption: Heartbeats, suspicion, gossip, then quorum.

quiz.q: A fixed 5 s heartbeat timeout works in the data center but fires constantly on a cross-region link. What does a phi-accrual detector change?
options: It sends heartbeats more often so silence is shorter
It judges silence against the observed arrival pattern, so tolerance adapts to jitter
It removes the need for heartbeats by using gossip
It guarantees a suspected node is really dead
quiz.why: Phi compares the current silence with the learned arrival pattern, so the same threshold tolerates longer gaps on a jittery link and shorter ones on a steady link, instead of one fixed number for both.

quiz.q: A 1,000-node cluster gossips once per second and each node contacts one random peer. About how long until a rumor reaches nearly everyone?
quiz.why: About log2(1000), around 10, plus several rounds for stragglers, so a bit under 20 rounds.

quiz.q: A node freezes for 20 s in a GC pause, is marked down, then resumes. What does this show about failure detectors?
options: Heartbeats should be sent over TCP
Slow and dead are indistinguishable from outside, so verdicts are suspicions that can be wrong
Gossip should have blocked the verdict
quiz.why: From a peer's view a paused node and a crashed node look identical, so any detector can only suspect and must tolerate being wrong.

quiz.q: A 5-node cluster partitions into groups of 3 and 2. Which rule prevents two leaders?
options: Only the group with at least 3 of the 5 configured members may lead
Both groups elect a leader, then merge by timestamp
The group whose heartbeats are fastest leads
The group containing the original leader always leads
quiz.why: Requiring a strict majority of the full membership means two disjoint groups can never both qualify, so at most one side can lead or commit.

cheatsheet.def: A small periodic message meaning I am alive. Receivers track the time of the last one; missing beats raise suspicion.
Declare a node dead after N seconds of silence. Simple, but one value cannot suit both fast LANs and jittery WANs.
A detector outputting a continuous suspicion score from learned heartbeat timing. Phi 8 is about a one-in-100-million chance of a false alarm under the model.
Each round, every node swaps state with a few random peers. Spreads news in about log N rounds with flat per-node load.
Each node's view of who is in the cluster and whether they look up or down, versioned so newer facts win in gossip. New nodes join via a seed node and spread by gossip.
A healthy node wrongly marked down, often after a GC pause or network blip. Aggressive thresholds cause flapping.
Two partitions both act as the authority and accept conflicting writes. Prevent with majority quorums.
More than half of the configured members, e.g. 3 of 5. Any two majorities overlap, so only one side can proceed.
